The Oriental magpie-robin (Copsychus saularis) is a widespread tropical passerine whose reproductive output has been quantified across its range. Field studies indicate that breeding females typically produce clutches containing 2 to 5 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 2 to 5 eggs per nesting attempt], and they commonly raise two broods during a single breeding season [F_R_i = two broods during a single breeding season]. These measurements were recorded from populations experiencing the warm ambient conditions of their native habitat at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The initial starting point for each offspring begins with a freshly laid egg weighing approximately 3.96 grams [Ww0 = approximately 3.96 grams], a figure derived from standard volumetric calculations based on an average egg length of 23.6 millimeters and a width of 17.9 millimeters. This modest initial wet mass is characteristic of the relatively small eggs produced by many muscicapid flycatchers and their allies, and it reflects the altricial developmental strategy typical of the group.

Developmental milestones in this species are closely tied to thermal conditions during the incubation and early nestling periods. Eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C] hatch after an incubation period lasting 12.5 days [ab = 12.5 days], a duration that aligns well with the values reported for other congeners in lowland tropical environments. The exact timing of hatching is critical for synchronizing the subsequent parental provisioning efforts, as the altricial nestlings emerge entirely dependent upon their parents for both warmth and food delivery. Following hatching, the young chicks embark on a rapid growth trajectory within the nest, where they are brooded intensively by the female while the male supplies food. The precise age at which these nestlings achieve fledging and depart the nest has been documented under typical active-season body temperatures of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], and it represents a key transition point in the life cycle.

Under the sustained high body temperatures characteristic of active metabolic periods, which average 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the developmental schedule unfolds with notable precision. Nestlings typically achieve their first flight and depart the nest at 16 days after hatching [tx = 16 days after hatching], marking the transition from a dependent nestling chick to a fledgling capable of short-distance movements at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This fledging period is relatively abbreviated compared to some temperate-dwelling congeners of similar body mass, possibly reflecting the reduced predation pressure or more predictable food supply in the tropical environments this species favours. Once independent from the nest, the juveniles enter a prolonged phase of somatic growth and feather development before they can attain full adult plumage. The period between fledging and the onset of reproductive capability is a critical window during which young birds must acquire the foraging skills and body condition necessary to compete for territories later in life.

The timing of sexual maturation in this species is another life-history parameter that has received empirical attention in the literature. Puberty, defined as the capacity to produce functional gametes, is achieved relatively quickly after the nestling phase ends. Under the typical thermal regime of active metabolism recorded at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], individuals attain sexual maturity at 48 days after hatching [tp = 48 days after hatching], a remarkably short interval that underscores the rapid life-history pace of this tropical insectivore. Despite this early gonadal maturation, the actual onset of first breeding activity is delayed considerably beyond the point of physiological puberty. The elapsed time from birth to the production of a first brood is substantially longer, reflecting the need for territory establishment, pair bond formation, and the accumulation of sufficient energetic reserves to support egg production and incubation. This delay between reaching puberty and initiating reproduction is a common pattern observed in territorial songbirds, where competition for high-quality breeding sites imposes a significant constraint on early reproductive output.

The first successful breeding event for an individual typically occurs at 401.5 days after hatching [tR = 401.5 days after hatching] under the prevailing metabolic body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a value that integrates both the physiological readiness of the bird and the ecological constraints of territory acquisition. This deferred reproduction is balanced by a relatively long potential lifespan, with the oldest documented individuals reaching 10 years [am = 10 years] under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The ultimate adult body mass attained by females is approximately 43 grams [Wwi = approximately 43 grams], a size that places the species in the mid-range for tropical insectivorous passerines. Metabolic rates measured during peak activity periods further illuminate the energetic demands of this lifestyle; at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum basal oxygen consumption recorded in active individuals reaches 64.85 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 64.85 milliliters of oxygen per hour], while a slightly lower value of 41.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 41.5 milliliters per hour] has been documented under the same thermal conditions. Together, these measurements provide a comprehensive portrait of the life-history strategy employed by this adaptable and widespread avian species.
